sentences: This is Uemura Shōen's Flame.
A woman in a kimono holds a strand of her black hair between her teeth as she turns to look back at us over her shoulder.
On a silk panel almost two meters tall, she stands entirely alone against an empty ground.
Born in Kyoto, Shōen was famous for serene, graceful paintings of beautiful women, and she later became the first woman to receive Japan's Order of Culture.
In 1918, during a difficult time in her life, she chose a subject utterly unlike her usual work.
Her face is pale and her teeth are blackened.
She is Lady Rokujō from the Noh play Aoi no Ue, adapted from The Tale of Genji.
Her jealousy turns her into a living spirit that leaves her body and torments her rival, Lady Aoi.
Look closely at her narrowed, downcast eyes.
Her Noh teacher, Kongō Iwao, told her that the deigan mask has gold in its eyes.
So she painted gold onto the back of the silk, making this woman's eyes glint as if with tears.
The strand of hair caught between her teeth is wound around her fingertips and pulled down.
With this single gesture, as if to bite the hair through, Shōen shows jealousy boiling over.
The slender, elegant fingers make it more chilling.
Her black hair streams down her back and half covers her body.
Painted strand by strand, it ripples like a troubled mind.
Against the pale robe, this dark current becomes a line that divides the picture from top to bottom.
Her white robe bears wisteria and a spider-web pattern.
Fine webs are strung between the yellow and purple blossoms.
Delicate flowers caught in a clinging web add to the unsettling mood.
Wisteria, too, is a vine that clings and twines around whatever it touches.
Now let your eyes move down to the hem.
The edge of her robe and her feet fade softly away into the silk.
With no feet showing, she seems not to touch the ground at all.
It is a quiet sign that this is not a living body, but a spirit that has left its body behind.
She showed it at the 12th Bunten, the Ministry of Education's annual art exhibition, in 1918.
Shōen is said to have called it her one and only painting of terrible, haunting beauty.
Today it belongs to the Tokyo National Museum.
Step back and see her whole figure once more.
Beauty and dread share this one silk panel.
Was it hatred that made her what she is, or a love she could never bring herself to let go?
